title: Continuous Integration and Delivery
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of continuous integration and delivery in a C#/.NET program.
Predict the result of the included C# example and verify the documented output.
Apply continuous integration and delivery to a small task and identify one relevant boundary, limitation, or version requirement.

content.intro: Continuous Integration and Delivery is lesson 187 in Security, Reliability, and Production Practices. Tests make intended behavior executable. Unit tests target small logic; integration tests verify that real components cooperate across a boundary.
content.why_it_matters: Production quality includes safe failure behavior, observable operation, and a repeatable way to ship updates. This lesson focuses on continuous integration and delivery and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Tests make intended behavior executable. Unit tests target small logic; integration tests verify that real components cooperate across a boundary.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for continuous integration and delivery. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Running tests in CI
items.text: Arrange known inputs, act once, and assert an observable outcome; keep tests independent and repeatable.

items.title: Build and deployment environments
items.text: Production behavior must fail safely and be observable. Validate untrusted input, enforce authorization at the server boundary, protect secrets, retry only appropriate transient failures, and verify the released artifact.

content_blocks.title: Version and reliability note
content_blocks.text: Tests make intended behavior executable. Unit tests target small logic; integration tests verify that real components cooperate across a boundary.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates continuous integration and delivery. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates continuous integration and delivery rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for continuous integration and delivery before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
